# Materials and Methods {#sec-annex-methods}

## Source Reconstruction Pipeline {#sec-annex-pipeline}

### Source Space {#sec-annex-source}

This section details the source space described in @sec-source-space.

#### Dipole Placement {#sec-annex-source-placement}

We reconstructed each subject's cortical surface with FreeSurfer (v7.4.1) and placed dipoles on it with MNE-Python (v1.9.0; @gramfort_meg_2013), using an oct6 (recursively subdivided octahedron) source space from which we excluded medial-wall and non-cortical vertices. Across the 31 subjects in the three studies, the resulting source spaces contained 7,275–7,660 dipoles per subject (mean 7,580), with a mean nearest-neighbor spacing of 2.89–3.57 mm (mean 3.30 mm).

#### Fixed Orientations {#sec-annex-source-orientation}

We fixed each dipole's orientation normal to the cortical surface. This constraint is standard in distributed source reconstruction because pyramidal neurons, the dominant contributors to the EEG signal, have net dipole moments oriented normal to the surface [@dale_improved_1993]. For the connectivity-informed methods, the constraint is also a structural requirement. The connectome specifies whether two cortical locations are connected, so it can couple one scalar amplitude at location A with one at location B. A free-orientation dipole, however, has three orthogonal components at each location, and the connectome does not specify how A's components couple to B's.

### Volume Conduction Model {#sec-annex-bem}

This section details the head model described in @sec-bem.

#### Head-Model Pipeline {#sec-annex-bem-pipeline}

Brain tissues were segmented into three compartments (inner skull, outer skull, scalp) using the SimNIBS CHARM pipeline (v4.5; @puonti_accurate_2020). Each compartment mask was smoothed via morphological closing and fitted with a deformable grade-5 icosahedral template, each surface constrained in turn to stay outside its inner neighbor's already-fitted surface (skin fitted last, constrained by the outer skull; outer skull constrained by the inner skull) — the "sequential and non-intersecting" fitting referenced in the main text.

#### Skull-Base Limitation {#sec-annex-bem-skull-base}

We segmented the head into three compartments, bounded by the inner skull, outer skull and scalp surfaces, using the SimNIBS CHARM pipeline (v4.5; @puonti_accurate_2020). We smoothed each compartment mask by morphological closing. To extract the mask's boundary, we started from a sphere tessellated as a grade-5 icosahedron (10,242 vertices) and deformed it iteratively until it enclosed the mask, closely following its boundary. We fitted the surfaces sequentially from the inside out, constraining each to stay outside the surface fitted before it: first the inner skull, then the outer skull, and finally the scalp. The main text refers to this procedure as "sequential and non-intersecting" fitting.

#### Comparison with MNE-Python's Watershed Extraction {#sec-annex-bem-watershed}

MNE-Python's default pipeline (`mne.bem.make_watershed_bem`) calls FreeSurfer's `mri_watershed`, which fits only the scalp surface directly to the T1-weighted image, by deforming a grade-5 icosahedral surface around the head. Because bone has poor contrast on T1-weighted MRI, `mri_watershed` approximates the two skull surfaces instead of detecting the bone boundary: it obtains the inner skull by growing the brain surface outward by 3 mm, and the outer skull by shrinking the scalp surface inward by 3 mm [@freesurfer_mri_watershed_nodate]. These heuristic surfaces are a well-known source of geometry errors. FreeSurfer itself describes them as a convenience rather than a high-quality estimate of the tissue boundaries, and MNE's documentation recommends inspecting them visually before use. These errors motivated the CHARM-based pipeline we use in this manuscript.

To illustrate these errors, we also ran MNE-Python's default watershed extraction (`mne.bem.make_watershed_bem`, FreeSurfer v7.4.1) on the sample subject used for simulation and compared its surfaces with the CHARM-based surfaces we used for reconstruction (@tbl-annex-bem-comparison). The watershed geometry fails MNE's own BEM-construction check: `mne.make_bem_model` raises `RuntimeError: Surface inner skull is not completely inside surface outer skull`. A direct nesting check of each pair of adjacent surfaces shows why. 42/10,242 (0.41%) inner-skull vertices lie outside the outer-skull surface, so the two skull surfaces intersect, and 4/10,242 (0.04%) outer-skull vertices lie outside the scalp. Because the CHARM-based pipeline fits each surface outside the previous one, it produces no such violations: its skull surfaces are at least 2.32 mm apart, and its BEM model builds without error.

| Metric | MNE default watershed | Custom CHARM pipeline |
|:---|---:|---:|
| Inner-skull vertices outside outer-skull | 42 / 10,242 (0.41%) | 0 / 10,242 (0.00%) |
| Outer-skull vertices outside scalp | 4 / 10,242 (0.04%) | 0 / 10,242 (0.00%) |
| Minimum inner-to-outer-skull gap | 0 mm | 2.32 mm |
| Minimum outer-skull-to-scalp gap | 2.12 mm | 3.21 mm |
| `mne.make_bem_model` / `make_bem_solution` | Fails (nesting violation) | Succeeds |

: For the sample simulation subject, MNE-Python's default watershed extraction produces skull surfaces that intersect, whereas the CHARM-based pipeline used throughout this manuscript produces correctly nested surfaces. {#tbl-annex-bem-comparison}

In the simulation subject, the failure is easy to detect because MNE refuses to build the BEM model. Watershed geometry can also fail silently. For subject sub-pat10 of the epilepsy surgery cohort (Study II), the watershed surfaces pass MNE's nesting check (`mne.make_bem_model` and `mne.make_bem_solution` both run without error), yet they are visibly wrong (@fig-annex-bem-spike). Panel (a) shows CHARM's tissue segmentation (`Bone-Cortical` and `Bone-Cancellous` in tan; `Skin` not shown) as an anatomical reference for the skull. This segmentation is not independent ground truth for the CHARM surface in panel (b), which is fitted to it. It is, however, a fair check of the watershed surface in panel (c), which never uses it. CHARM's outer-skull contour (b) closely follows the segmented bone boundary. The watershed contour (c) does not: it balloons well beyond the segmented bone, consistent with a surface obtained by growing the brain surface and shrinking the scalp rather than by detecting bone.

#### Forward-Model Mismatch {#sec-annex-forward}

Study I simulates the EEG with one forward model and reconstructs it with another, which avoids the inverse crime (@sec-data-synthetic). We quantify the mismatch between the two with the relative difference measure (RDM) of @dannhauer_modeling_2011, who compared simplified skull models against a detailed reference in both forward computation and dipole localization.


```{python filename="forward_mismatch_stats.py"}
#| output: false
import sys
import numpy as np
sys.path.insert(0, "..")
from scripts.data_manager import SimfManager

# Self-contained, like the other Annex sections above: reloads the two
# forward solutions actually used for Study I (Volume Conduction Model) rather than
# hand-computing this offline - processing_simf.qmd does not itself compute
# this comparison, so there is no cached result to reuse here.
dm_fwd = SimfManager("../processing/simf.config.yml")
sub_fwd = "10"
fwd_sim = dm_fwd.load(sub_fwd, "fwd", desc="sim")
fwd_inv = dm_fwd.load(sub_fwd, "fwd", desc="inv")

G_sim = fwd_sim["sol"]["data"]
G_inv = fwd_inv["sol"]["data"]

# Relative difference measure (RDM): per-dipole leadfield columns normalized
# to unit norm (removing amplitude scaling), then the norm of their
# difference - a standard forward-model comparison metric quantifying
# topographic (shape) mismatch, of the kind used in the head-model-mismatch
# literature (@dannhauer_modeling_2011). 0 = identical topography, 2 = inverted.
G_sim_n = G_sim / np.linalg.norm(G_sim, axis=0, keepdims=True)
G_inv_n = G_inv / np.linalg.norm(G_inv, axis=0, keepdims=True)
rdm = np.linalg.norm(G_sim_n - G_inv_n, axis=0)

fwd_n_dipoles = f"{G_sim.shape[1]:,}"
fwd_rdm_median = fmt_num(np.median(rdm) * 100, 1)
fwd_rdm_mean = fmt_num(np.mean(rdm) * 100, 1)
fwd_rdm_iqr_lo = fmt_num(np.percentile(rdm, 25) * 100, 1)
fwd_rdm_iqr_hi = fmt_num(np.percentile(rdm, 75) * 100, 1)
```

To quantify how much our two forward models differ, we compared their gain matrices for the sample subject used for simulation (7465-dipole source space). We used the relative difference measure (RDM), a standard metric for comparing forward models that captures differences in topography (shape) independently of amplitude. Topography is the relevant measure of mismatch here: a reconstruction method that is invariant to overall amplitude scaling would not be biased by differences in gain amplitude alone. Across dipoles, the RDM has a median of `{python} fwd_rdm_median`% (mean `{python} fwd_rdm_mean`%, IQR [`{python} fwd_rdm_iqr_lo`%, `{python} fwd_rdm_iqr_hi`%]), consistent with the ~10% mismatch quoted in the main text.

### Structural Connectome and Graph Harmonics {#sec-annex-connectome}

This section provides implementation-level detail for the connectomes and surrogates described in @sec-connectome.

#### Empirical Connectome {#sec-annex-connectome-empirical}

Short-range links connect each dipole to its geodesically nearest neighbors on the cortical surface, under two constraints: each neighbor must lie within 15 mm geodesic distance, and each dipole has at most 8 neighbors. These links mainly ensure that every dipole is connected: tractography alone leaves 54 of the simulation subject's 7,465 dipoles (0.7%) without any edge. We chose the 15 mm threshold so that every dipole has at least one short-range neighbor even without tractography, since no dipole lies farther than 13.5 mm from its nearest neighbor. This threshold also lies well within the 3–30 mm range estimated for U-fiber length [@movahedian_attar_mapping_2020]. A dipole has about 88 candidate neighbors within 15 mm; the 8-neighbor cap, whose value we chose arbitrarily, keeps the number of short-range edges small. Where tractography already links two dipoles, the tractography edge replaces the short-range one. Of the 28,458 short-range edges, 20,322 (71%) coincide with a tractography edge, so short-range links add only 8,136 edges, 4.3% of the 188,890 edges in the final connectome.

#### Atlas Surrogate {#sec-annex-connectome-atlas}


This section details the atlas surrogate (@tbl-surrogates), which replaces the individual connectome when no diffusion MRI is available: in Studies II and III (@sec-data-resection, @sec-data-ieeg), and in the surrogate comparison of Study I (@sec-s1-surrogates). The main text introduces it in @sec-connectome.

The atlas surrogate takes its long-range tracts from the MultiConn atlas, whose reference population comprises 66 subjects, and retains only tracts present in all 66. Within each pair of atlas-connected regions, it does not connect every pair of dipoles. Instead, it keeps the 14% of dipole pairs that lie closest to each other in Euclidean distance (rounded, with at least one pair per region pair), so the selection is deterministic. We set this percentage to match the edge density of the simulation subject's empirical connectome (described above), because that subject is the only one in our sample with diffusion MRI. Each kept edge is weighted by a fiber length equal to the atlas's mean fiber length for the region pair plus the edge's extra distance relative to the closest dipole pair. The closest pair therefore receives exactly the atlas length, and every other pair is longer by its extra distance.

#### Local Surrogate {#sec-annex-connectome-local}

The local surrogate keeps only the short-range links of the individual connectome (@sec-sec-annex-connectome-empirical): each dipole connects to at most 8 geodesically nearest neighbors within 15 mm on the cortical surface. Short-range links never cross the midline, so on their own they leave the two hemispheres disconnected. To obtain a connected graph, we also link dipoles across the hemispheres, but only between homotopic regions (the same region in the left and right hemispheres): two dipoles are linked if they belong to homotopic regions and the Euclidean distance between them is below 30 mm. This yields a connected graph in every subject.

#### Laplace–Beltrami Surrogate (GBF) {#sec-annex-connectome-beltrami}

We computed Laplace–Beltrami eigenmodes with the `lapy` Python library (v1.6.0), which solves the eigenproblem with the finite-element method. We computed them on the triangulated source space itself (@sec-source-space), the decimated, cortex-only surface that carries the dipoles, rather than on the dense FreeSurfer surface usually used for this computation. The eigenmodes of @wang_geometry_2026 are likewise defined on a downsampled source space, with ~10,000 dipoles per hemisphere for real data and ~4,000 per hemisphere for their benchmark simulations, comparable to our ~3,800 per hemisphere.


### Inverse Problem and Methods {#sec-annex-inverse}

This section details the inverse methods described in @sec-inverse.

#### Solver {#sec-annex-solvers}

The five methods with a Gaussian prior ($p = 2$), namely wMNE, dSPM, sLORETA, wCSET and GBF, all compute Eq. (2) with the same procedure, based on a singular value decomposition (SVD) as in MNE-Python [@gramfort_meg_2013]. For wMNE, dSPM and sLORETA, we used MNE-Python's implementation (`make_inverse_operator`, `apply_inverse`). For wCSET and GBF, we used our own implementation of the same steps, because these two methods require a non-diagonal prior, which MNE-Python does not accept.

**Whitening.** Let $\mathbf P$ be the average-reference projector and $\mathbf W_n$ the whitener derived from the noise covariance, so that the whitened noise has identity covariance. The whitened data and gain matrix are $\mathbf y_w = \mathbf W_n \mathbf P \mathbf y$ and $\mathbf L_w = \mathbf W_n \mathbf P \mathbf L$. Let $r$ be the rank of the noise covariance after projection.

**Prior factor.** We write the source covariance as $\mathbf\Sigma_{\mathbf s} = \mathbf B \mathbf B^\top$, with

$$
\mathbf B =
\begin{cases}
\mathbf I & \text{dSPM, sLORETA,}\\
\mathbf W_d & \text{wMNE,}\\
\mathbf W_d\,\mathbf U\,\mathbf W_h & \text{wCSET and GBF.}
\end{cases}
$$

Here $\mathbf W_d$ is a diagonal depth-weighting matrix computed from the whitened gain matrix, $W_{d,ii} = \lVert [\mathbf L_w]_{:,i} \rVert^{-\kappa}$. The matrices $\mathbf U$ and $\mathbf W_h$ are specific to wCSET and GBF and are defined below. For wMNE, we set $\kappa = 2$ rather than MNE-Python's default of 0.8, which is intended for MEG: for EEG, @lin_assessing_2006 found values of 2 to 5 optimal. dSPM and sLORETA use no depth weighting, since their standardization already compensates for the depth bias.

**Scaling.** We then replace $\mathbf B$ by $c\,\mathbf B$, with $c = \sqrt{r / \lVert \mathbf L_w \mathbf B \rVert_F^2}$, so that $\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf L_w \mathbf\Sigma_{\mathbf s} \mathbf L_w^\top) = r$. On average, the prior then predicts the same power per whitened channel as the noise. This puts the regularization parameter $\alpha$ on the same scale for every method.

**SVD and solution.** Let

$$
\mathbf L_w \mathbf B = \mathbf E_f \mathbf \Gamma \mathbf E_\ell^\top, \qquad \mathbf \Gamma = \operatorname{diag}(\gamma_1, \dots, \gamma_m),
$$

be the SVD of the weighted gain matrix, where $m$ is the number of channels, so that $\mathbf E_f$ is square and orthogonal. Substituting $\mathbf\Sigma_{\mathbf s} = \mathbf B \mathbf B^\top$ into the linear operator of Eq. (2) and using $\mathbf E_f \mathbf E_f^\top = \mathbf I$ gives

$$
\mathbf\Sigma_{\mathbf s} \mathbf L_w^\top (\mathbf L_w \mathbf\Sigma_{\mathbf s} \mathbf L_w^\top + \alpha \mathbf I)^{-1}
= \mathbf B\,\mathbf E_\ell \mathbf\Gamma \mathbf E_f^\top \big(\mathbf E_f (\mathbf\Gamma^2 + \alpha \mathbf I) \mathbf E_f^\top\big)^{-1}
= \mathbf B\,\mathbf E_\ell\,\mathbf D_\alpha\,\mathbf E_f^\top,
\qquad \mathbf D_\alpha = \operatorname{diag}\!\left(\frac{\gamma_j}{\gamma_j^2 + \alpha}\right).
$$

The estimate is therefore

$$
\mathbf s^* = \mathbf B\,\mathbf E_\ell\,\mathbf D_\alpha\,\mathbf E_f^\top \mathbf y_w.
$$

A zero singular value, such as the one introduced by the average reference, gives a zero entry in $\mathbf D_\alpha$ and so contributes nothing. We compute the SVD once per forward model and prior.

**wCSET.** For wCSET, $\mathbf U$ contains the eigenvectors of the normalized Laplacian of the connectome (@sec-connectome), with graph frequencies $\lambda_i \in [0, 2]$, $W_{h,ii} = e^{-\beta \lambda_i}$ with $\beta = 5$, and $\mathbf W_d$ uses $\kappa = 0.2$. Written out in full, the estimate is

$$
\mathbf s^*_{\text{wCSET}} = c\,\mathbf W_d \mathbf U \mathbf W_h\,\mathbf E_\ell\,\mathbf D_\alpha\,\mathbf E_f^\top \mathbf y_w,
\qquad \mathbf L_w\,(c\,\mathbf W_d \mathbf U \mathbf W_h) = \mathbf E_f \mathbf\Gamma \mathbf E_\ell^\top,
$$

with source covariance $\mathbf\Sigma_{\mathbf s} = c^2\,\mathbf W_d \mathbf U \mathbf W_h^2 \mathbf U^\top \mathbf W_d$. Because $\mathbf U$ is orthogonal and $\mathbf W_d$ and $\mathbf W_h$ have positive diagonals, $\mathbf B$ is invertible. This estimate is therefore the exact minimizer of Eq. (3) with $\alpha$ replaced by $\alpha / c^2$.

**GBF.** For GBF, $\mathbf W_d = \mathbf I$, and $\mathbf U$ holds the Laplace–Beltrami eigenmodes of the cortical mesh, with eigenvalues $0 = \mu_1 \le \mu_2 \le \dots$. @wang_geometry_2026 give mode $i$ the prior variance $-\ln(\mu_i)/\beta$ (their Eq. 5), keep the first $S = 300$ modes, and use $\beta$ as their regularization parameter. We adapted this prior to our solver in two ways.

First, we normalize the eigenvalues by $\mu_S$ and floor them at $10^{-8}$. Since $\mathbf\Sigma_{\mathbf s} = \mathbf B \mathbf B^\top$, the harmonic weights are the square roots of the resulting variances:

$$
W_{h,ii} =
\begin{cases}
\sqrt{-\ln \tilde\mu_i} & i \le S,\\
0 & i > S,
\end{cases}
\qquad \tilde\mu_i = \max\!\left(\frac{\mu_i}{\mu_S},\, 10^{-8}\right).
$$

The normalization ensures $\tilde\mu_i \le 1$, so every weight is real and none depends on the units of $\mu_i$. The floor keeps the weight of the constant mode ($\mu_1 = 0$) finite, a case that @wang_geometry_2026 do not discuss. The weights decrease as $\mu_i$ increases and reach zero at mode $S$, since $\tilde\mu_S = 1$. $\mathbf B$ is therefore singular, and our estimate is confined to the first $S - 1$ modes, whereas @wang_geometry_2026 give all $S$ modes a nonzero weight.

Second, we drop $\beta$. The solver of @wang_geometry_2026 has no separate regularization parameter, so $\beta$, by scaling the whole prior, also sets the regularization: it plays the role of our $\alpha$. In our solver, the scaling $c$ cancels any constant factor such as $\beta$, and our own rule sets $\alpha$ (@sec-lambda). Their tuned $\beta$ therefore no longer applies, and neither does $S = 300$, which they chose together with it. So as not to disadvantage GBF, we retuned $S$, the only remaining GBF parameter that affects the estimate, and used $S = 150$ (@sec-annex-tuning).


#### Parameter Tuning of CSET, wCSET and GBF {#sec-annex-tuning}

::: {.callout-warning title="To write"}
CSET's fixed $\alpha = 0.1$ and its depth-weighting exponent $\kappa = 0.2$ (promised in @sec-inverse and @sec-lambda), tuned on the same spikes as wCSET and GBF below.
:::

```{python filename="tuning_stats.py"}
#| output: false
# Tuning sweep of wCSET (beta x kappa) and GBF (cutoff S): notebooks/tuning_sweep.ipynb, on the 50
# tuning spikes of notebooks/simulate_tuning_spikes.py. Metrics as in Study I: localization error at
# the quarter-rising phase (qrp) and spatial correlation, here averaged over the reconstruction window.
# Paired comparisons: Wilcoxon signed-rank (zeros kept, Pratt), one spike = one pair, uncorrected.
import pandas as pd
from scipy.stats import wilcoxon

TUNING = "../results/simf/tuning"
tun = pd.read_csv(f"{TUNING}/tuning_sweep_paper-metrics.tsv", sep="\t")
tun_regions = pd.read_csv(f"{TUNING}/tuning-regions.csv")["region"]
tun_n = tun.run.nunique()
tun_n_lh = int(tun_regions.str.startswith("ctx-lh").sum())
tun_n_rh = len(tun_regions) - tun_n_lh
tun_qrp_ms = fmt_num(tun.qrp_time.median() * 1000, 0)
tun_pp_ms = fmt_num(tun.pp_time.median() * 1000, 0)

tun["cfg"] = [
    f"{b:g}/{k:g}" if m == "wcset" else (f"{p} {int(S)}" if m == "gbf" else m)
    for m, b, k, p, S in zip(tun.method, tun.beta, tun.depth, tun.prior, tun.S)
]
tun_loc = tun.pivot_table(index="run", columns="cfg", values="loc_err_qrp")
tun_corr = tun.pivot_table(index="run", columns="cfg", values="corr_mean")

def tun_p(table, a, b):
    return wilcoxon(table[a], table[b], zero_method="pratt").pvalue

def tun_share(table, a, b, higher_is_better):
    """% of spikes where a is better than b."""
    better = table[a] > table[b] if higher_is_better else table[a] < table[b]
    return fmt_num(100 * better.mean(), 0)

med = lambda c: fmt_num(tun_loc[c].median())
mean_le = lambda c: fmt_num(tun_loc[c].mean())
r = lambda c: fmt_stat(tun_corr[c].mean(), 3)

# wCSET
w_le_ref, w_le_ref_mean, w_r_ref = med("5/0.2"), mean_le("5/0.2"), r("5/0.2")
w_le_b10, w_le_b10_k0, w_le_b5_k0 = med("10/0.2"), med("10/0"), med("5/0")
w_r_b10_k0 = r("10/0")
w_p_le_b10 = fmt_p(tun_p(tun_loc, "10/0", "5/0"))
w_p_le_b10_k02 = fmt_p(tun_p(tun_loc, "10/0.2", "5/0.2"))
w_k_bad = [c for c in tun_corr if "/" in c and float(c.split("/")[1]) >= 0.5]
w_k_bad_share = fmt_num(min(100 * (tun_corr[c] < tun_corr["5/0.2"]).mean() for c in w_k_bad if c.startswith(("3/", "5/", "7/"))), 0)
w_b1_le = fmt_num(tun_loc[[c for c in tun_loc if c.startswith("1/")]].median().min())
w_k0_dr = fmt_stat((tun_corr["5/0"] - tun_corr["5/0.2"]).mean(), 3)
w_k0_share = tun_share(tun_corr, "5/0", "5/0.2", True)
w_k0_p_r = fmt_p(tun_p(tun_corr, "5/0", "5/0.2"))
w_k0_p_le = fmt_p(tun_p(tun_loc, "5/0", "5/0.2"))
w_k0_le_mean = mean_le("5/0")

# GBF
g_le_150, g_le_200, g_r_150, g_r_200 = med("normalized 150"), med("normalized 200"), r("normalized 150"), r("normalized 200")
g_p_le_200 = fmt_p(tun_p(tun_loc, "normalized 200", "normalized 150"))
g_p_r_200 = fmt_p(tun_p(tun_corr, "normalized 200", "normalized 150"))
g_p_r_300 = fmt_p(tun_p(tun_corr, "normalized 300", "normalized 150"))
g_r_600, g_le_600 = r("normalized 600"), med("normalized 600")
g_share_600 = tun_share(tun_corr, "normalized 150", "normalized 600", True)
g_raw = [c for c in tun_corr if c.startswith("raw")]
g_raw_share = min(100 * (tun_corr[c] < tun_corr[c.replace("raw", "normalized")]).mean() for c in g_raw)
g_raw_share = "in every spike" if g_raw_share == 100 else f"in at least {g_raw_share:.0f}% of spikes"
g_sl_le, g_sl_r = med("sloreta"), r("sloreta")
_r_low = tun_corr[[f"normalized {S}" for S in (50, 100, 150, 200)]].mean()
g_r_lo_200, g_r_hi_200 = fmt_stat(_r_low.min(), 3), fmt_stat(_r_low.max(), 3)
_g150 = pd.read_csv(f"{TUNING}/tuning_gbf_summary_paper-metrics.tsv", sep="\t").query("prior == 'normalized' and S == 150").iloc[0]
g_lh_150, g_rh_150 = int(_g150.S_lh), int(_g150.S_rh)

# Domain of the unnormalized prior sqrt(-ln mu): the Laplace-Beltrami eigenvalues used by the sweep
import numpy as np
sys.path.insert(0, "..")
from scripts.data_manager import SimfManager
mu = np.asarray(SimfManager("../processing/simf.config.yml").load("10", "eig", desc="beltrami")["val"])
g_raw_smax = max(int(c.split()[1]) for c in g_raw)
g_n_zero = int((mu < 1e-8).sum())
g_mu_smax = fmt_stat(mu[g_raw_smax - 1], 2)
g_raw_smax_txt = str(g_raw_smax)
g_first_mu1 = f"{int(np.argmax(mu >= 1)) + 1:,}"
```

**Tuning spikes.** We tuned the parameters on a separate set of `{python} tun_n` simulated spikes, generated with exactly the simulation of Study I (@sec-data-synthetic): the same subject, head models, connectome, spike waveform, propagation model, noise and SNR. Each spike starts in a different cortical region (`{python} tun_n_lh` in the left hemisphere, `{python} tun_n_rh` in the right), chosen by farthest-point sampling. Study I uses all other cortical regions, so tuning and evaluation do not overlap. We reconstructed each spike with the solvers of @sec-annex-solvers, with the same preprocessing and regularization rule as in Study I, and scored it with Study I's metrics (@sec-metrics): the localization error at the time the EEG reaches 25% of its peak amplitude (a median of `{python} tun_qrp_ms` ms after onset, the peak being at `{python} tun_pp_ms` ms), and the spatial correlation with the simulated activity, averaged over the reconstruction window (−20 to 150 ms). Paired comparisons between settings use the Wilcoxon signed-rank test across spikes; with one test per comparison and no correction, their p-values are descriptive only.

**wCSET.** We varied the harmonic decay $\beta \in \{1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10\}$ and the depth-weighting exponent $\kappa \in \{0, 0.2, 0.5, 0.8, 1\}$, using the empirical connectome of Study I (@fig-annex-tuning-wcset). Weak decay ($\beta = 1$) performed worst on both metrics, with a median localization error of at least `{python} w_b1_le` mm. Strong depth weighting ($\kappa \ge 0.5$) lowered the correlation: for $\beta = 3$–7, it was below that of $\beta = 5$, $\kappa = 0.2$ in at least `{python} w_k_bad_share`% of spikes. Among the remaining settings, the two metrics pull $\beta$ in opposite directions. The correlation rose steadily with $\beta$, from `{python} w_r_ref` at $\beta = 5$ to `{python} w_r_b10_k0` at $\beta = 10$ ($\kappa = 0$), presumably because a stronger low-pass spreads the reconstruction along the connectome, as the simulated activity spreads. The localization error, in contrast, is measured early in the spike, while activity is still confined to the initial patch, and it tended to worsen at large $\beta$. Its median rose from `{python} w_le_ref` mm at $\beta = 5$ to `{python} w_le_b10` mm at $\beta = 10$ with $\kappa = 0.2$ ($p$ `{python} w_p_le_b10_k02`), and from `{python} w_le_b5_k0` to `{python} w_le_b10_k0` mm with $\kappa = 0$ ($p$ `{python} w_p_le_b10`), although neither increase was significant. We therefore chose $\beta = 5$ as the best compromise between the two metrics.

At $\beta = 5$, removing depth weighting ($\kappa = 0$) raised the correlation slightly, by $\Delta r$ = `{python} w_k0_dr` (higher in `{python} w_k0_share`% of spikes; $p$ `{python} w_k0_p_r`), and did not significantly change the localization error (median `{python} w_le_b5_k0` mm with $\kappa = 0$ vs `{python} w_le_ref` mm with $\kappa = 0.2$, mean `{python} w_k0_le_mean` vs `{python} w_le_ref_mean` mm; $p$ `{python} w_k0_p_le`). We nevertheless kept $\kappa = 0.2$, the value used in all three studies: the gain from $\kappa = 0$ is less than a fifth of the non-inferiority margin for correlation ($\delta = 0.1$, @sec-stats), so it is unlikely to change any conclusion.

```{python filename="tuning_wcset_plot.py"}
#| label: fig-annex-tuning-wcset
#| fig-cap: "Tuning of wCSET's harmonic decay β and depth-weighting exponent κ on the 50 tuning spikes. (a) Median localization error at 25% of the spike's peak amplitude (lower is better). (b) Spatial correlation with the simulated activity, averaged over the reconstruction window and then over spikes (higher is better). The outlined cell is the setting used in the studies (β = 5, κ = 0.2)."
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle

w = tun[tun.method == "wcset"]
panels = [
    ("loc_err_qrp", "median", "a. Localization error at 25% of peak (mm)", "Greys", "{:.1f}"),
    ("corr_mean", "mean", "b. Spatial correlation, window mean", "Blues", "{:.3f}"),
]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.6))
for ax, (metric, agg, title, cmap, fmt) in zip(axes, panels):
    grid = w.pivot_table(index="depth", columns="beta", values=metric, aggfunc=agg)
    im = ax.imshow(grid.values, cmap=cmap, aspect="auto")
    norm = im.norm
    for i in range(grid.shape[0]):
        for j in range(grid.shape[1]):
            v = grid.values[i, j]
            ax.text(j, i, fmt.format(v), ha="center", va="center", fontsize=9,
                    color="white" if norm(v) > 0.6 else "#222222")
    ax.set_xticks(range(grid.shape[1]), [f"{b:g}" for b in grid.columns])
    ax.set_yticks(range(grid.shape[0]), [f"{k:g}" for k in grid.index])
    ax.set_xlabel("harmonic decay β")
    ax.set_ylabel("depth-weighting exponent κ")
    ax.set_title(title, loc="left", fontsize=11)
    j_ref, i_ref = list(grid.columns).index(5), list(grid.index).index(0.2)
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((j_ref - 0.5, i_ref - 0.5), 1, 1, fill=False, ec=COLORS["wcset"], lw=2.5))
    ax.tick_params(length=0)
    for side in ax.spines.values():
        side.set_visible(False)
    fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, fraction=0.04, pad=0.02).outline.set_visible(False)
plt.tight_layout()
```

**GBF cutoff.** We varied GBF's cutoff from $S = 50$ to $S = 4{,}000$, ranking the modes of both hemispheres together by eigenvalue (@tbl-annex-gbf-cutoff). Performance was best over a plateau from $S = 150$ to $S = 200$, mainly in localization error and in correlation at 25% of peak; the window-mean correlation varied little up to $S = 200$ (`{python} g_r_lo_200`–`{python} g_r_hi_200`). Within the plateau, $S = 200$ was equal to or slightly better than $S = 150$ on every metric, with a lower median localization error (`{python} g_le_200` vs `{python} g_le_150` mm) and the same correlation (`{python} g_r_200` vs `{python} g_r_150`), but neither difference was significant ($p$ `{python} g_p_le_200` and $p$ `{python} g_p_r_200`). Larger cutoffs lowered the correlation, from $S = 300$ on (vs $S = 150$; $p$ `{python} g_p_r_300`). At the cutoff of @wang_geometry_2026, about 300 modes per hemisphere ($S = 600$), the correlation fell to `{python} g_r_600`, below that of $S = 150$ in `{python} g_share_600`% of spikes.

We also evaluated the unnormalized prior of @wang_geometry_2026, $W_{h,ii} = \sqrt{-\ln \mu_i}$. This weight is infinite for $\mu_i = 0$ and imaginary for $\mu_i > 1$. The first case affects only the two constant modes, one per hemisphere, whose eigenvalues we floored at $10^{-8}$, as for the normalized prior. The second case does not arise at the cutoffs tested: the largest eigenvalue they keep (mode `{python} g_raw_smax_txt`) is `{python} g_mu_smax`, and $\mu_i$ exceeds 1 only from mode `{python} g_first_mu1` on, so every weight is real. At every cutoff tested, the unnormalized prior had a lower correlation than our normalized prior `{python} g_raw_share`, and a larger median localization error, so the normalization does not disadvantage GBF.

We kept $S = 150$, which retains `{python} g_lh_150` modes in the left hemisphere and `{python} g_rh_150` in the right. We had fixed this value in a preliminary tuning on a smaller set of simulations, before running the studies, and it lies on the plateau, where it did not differ significantly from $S = 200$.

Bold: the cutoff used in the studies."

## Datasets and Study-Specific Settings {#sec-annex-datasets}

### Synthetic Data (Study I) {#sec-annex-data-synthetic}

This section lists everything needed to reproduce the synthetic data of Study I (@sec-data-synthetic): the input data, the processing applied to them before simulation, and the simulation itself. The code for all three steps is in `processing_simf.qmd` in the manuscript repository ([github.com/NinoHerve/wCSET](https://github.com/NinoHerve/wCSET)).

#### VEPCON Data {#sec-annex-vepcon}

All subject data come from the VEPCON dataset [@pascucci_source_2022], publicly available on OpenNeuro as dataset ds003505 ([openneuro.org/datasets/ds003505](https://openneuro.org/datasets/ds003505)); the file paths below refer to snapshot 1.1.2. We use a single participant, `sub-10`, the subject used for simulation throughout this manuscript. We use none of VEPCON's EEG recordings or raw diffusion images, and no other participant. We also do not use VEPCON's FreeSurfer derivatives: we reran the FreeSurfer reconstruction (v7.4.1) on the raw T1-weighted image, with the processing code included in `processing_simf.qmd`.

| File (relative to the dataset root) | Content | Used for |
|:---|:---|:---|
| `sub-10/anat/sub-10_T1w.nii.gz` | Raw T1-weighted MRI | FreeSurfer reconstruction (source space, parcellation, electrode coregistration) and CHARM tissue segmentation (BEM) |
| `derivatives/cmp-v3.0.3/sub-10/dwi/sub-10_model-CSD_desc-DET_tractogram.trk` | Whole-brain tractogram, in diffusion space | Long-range connectome edges |
| `derivatives/cmp-v3.0.3/sub-10/xfm/final0GenericAffine.mat` | Affine registration between T1w and diffusion space (ANTs) | Mapping streamline endpoints to T1w space |

: VEPCON files required to reproduce the synthetic data, all for `sub-10`. {#tbl-annex-vepcon-files}

#### Tractogram {#sec-annex-tractogram}

We used the tractogram as distributed with VEPCON, without rerunning tractography. According to its Connectome Mapper 3 [@tourbier_connectome_2022] configuration file (`derivatives/cmp-v3.0.3/sub-10/sub-10_diffusion_config.json`), the pipeline corrected the diffusion data for eddy currents and motion (FSL `eddy_correct`) but applied no denoising or bias-field correction. It then reconstructed fiber orientations in MRtrix3 with constrained spherical deconvolution (CSD, maximum harmonic order 4) and generated one million streamlines with deterministic tractography (`SD_stream`; step 0.5 mm, length 5–200 mm, maximum angle 45°, FOD cutoff 0.05), without anatomically constrained tractography (ACT). Finally, it filtered the streamlines with SIFT, which kept 200,164 of them (20%).


#### External Resources {#sec-annex-external-resources}

Besides VEPCON, the pipeline uses three external resources:

- **Sensor layout:** the EGI 256-channel HydroCel template montage built into MNE-Python [@gramfort_meg_2013]. We use no subject-specific electrode positions.
- **Parcellation:** the Lausanne 2018 scale-4 cortical atlas [@cammoun_mapping_2012; @tourbier_connectome_2022] and the probabilistic thalamic-nuclei atlas built from Human Connectome Project data [@najdenovska_vivo_2018], together with the MNI ICBM152 2009c template [@fonov_unbiased_2011], from which we build the MultiConn parcellation [@aleman-gomez_multi-scale_2022]. The final parcellation keeps only cortical regions, but the code requires the thalamic atlas so that subcortical regions can be added in future work.
- **Atlas connectome:** the MultiConn probabilistic connectivity atlas at scale 4 [@aleman-gomez_multi-scale_2022], used only for the atlas surrogate (@sec-connectome).

**Electrodes.** We reduce the EGI template to 204 electrodes by removing the same cheek electrodes as in the epilepsy surgery data (@sec-data-resection). Because no fiducials were marked on `sub-10`'s MRI, MNE-Python estimates the nasion and preauricular points by mapping those of FreeSurfer's fsaverage through the subject's MNI transform. A rigid transformation (rotation and translation, no scaling) then aligns the template's fiducials with these estimates [@gramfort_meg_2013]. Finally, we project each electrode onto the CHARM scalp surface, along the ray from the surface's centroid through the electrode, so that every electrode lies on the scalp of the head model.

#### Processing Steps {#sec-annex-processing}

We derive all other inputs from the files above in five steps:

1. *Head model.* We segment the T1-weighted image with SimNIBS CHARM [@puonti_accurate_2020] and build the three BEM surfaces (inner skull, outer skull, scalp) from this segmentation (@sec-annex-bem).
2. *Parcellation.* We compute the MultiConn scale-4 parcellation on the FreeSurfer reconstruction, extending each cortical label 2 mm into the underlying white matter and thresholding the thalamic atlas at probability 0.05. The cortical labels define the cortex mask, which therefore also covers a 2 mm band of white matter beneath the cortex. They also define the 446 regions from which Study I's 100 source regions are drawn (@sec-data-synthetic).
3. *Source space.* We place dipoles on the FreeSurfer white-matter surface (oct6 spacing) and keep only those inside the cortex mask (@sec-annex-source).
4. *Electrodes.* We reduce the EGI template to 204 electrodes by removing the same cheek and neck electrodes as in the epilepsy surgery data (@sec-data-resection). Because no fiducials were marked on `sub-10`'s MRI, MNE-Python estimates the nasion and preauricular points by mapping those of FreeSurfer's fsaverage through the subject's MNI transform. A rigid transformation (rotation and translation, no scaling) then aligns the template's fiducials with these estimates [@gramfort_meg_2013]. Finally, we project each electrode onto the CHARM scalp surface, along the ray from the surface's centroid through the electrode, so that every electrode lies on the scalp of the head model.
5. *Connectome.* We map streamline endpoints from diffusion space to T1-weighted space with the ANTs affine transform (@tbl-annex-vepcon-files). We do not apply the nonlinear warp that completes this registration (`final1Warp.nii.gz`): its displacements are below 1 mm almost everywhere (median 0.08 mm, 99th percentile 1.0 mm) and at most 2.2 mm, below the 4 mm endpoint radius used next. We keep only streamlines whose two endpoints both fall in the cortex mask, and discard those with an endpoint farther than 4 mm from every dipole. We connect each endpoint to every dipole within 4 mm, not only to the nearest, so that a streamline links every dipole near one of its endpoints to every dipole near the other. We weight each edge by the mean length of the streamlines that link its two dipoles. Finally, we add short-range edges between neighboring dipoles where tractography found none (@sec-annex-connectome).

#### Simulation Parameters {#sec-annex-sim-params}

#### Simulation Parameters {#sec-annex-sim-params}

| Parameter | Symbol | Value | Unit | Description | Ref. |
|:---|:---:|---:|:---:|:---|:---:|
| Spike duration | $W$ | 0.05 | s | Total duration of the double-Hanning-window spike waveform | [@kane_revised_2017] |
| U-fiber length cutoff | $l_U$ | 30 | mm | Edges with length $l \le l_U$ are treated as U-fibers, longer edges as long-range tracts | [@movahedian_attar_mapping_2020] |
| Long-range conduction speed | $v_{\text{long}}$ | 4.5 | mm/ms | Conduction speed along edges with $l > l_U$ | [@lemarechal_brain_2022; @van_blooijs_developmental_2023] |
| U-fiber conduction speed | $v_U$ | 2.5 | mm/ms | Conduction speed along edges with $l \le l_U$ | [@van_blooijs_developmental_2023] |
| Nodal delay per hop | $\tau_p$ | 7 | ms | Time a cortical population takes to receive, integrate and re-fire an input; added once per edge along the propagation path | [@lemarechal_brain_2022] |
| Delay jitter per hop | $\sigma_\tau$ | 1 | ms | Standard deviation of the timing jitter added at each hop; after $n$ hops, the jitter has standard deviation $\sigma_\tau\sqrt{n}$, so arrival times are not locked to the sampling grid | — |
| Amplitude decay per hop | $\rho$ | 0.5 | — | Factor by which propagating activity is multiplied at each hop | — |
| Sensor noise floor | — | 2.0 | µV RMS | Fixed instrument and electrode noise, added at the sensors independently of the source-space noise | — |
| Total sensor noise (target) | — | 15.0 | µV RMS | Target RMS of all sensor-level background noise: the floor plus the forward-projected source-space noise | [@nunez_electric_2006] |
| SNR (target) | — | 5 | — | Target single-trial peak-amplitude SNR, used to scale the source activity before projection to the sensors | [@gonsisko_electroencephalographic_2024] |
| Source regions | — | 396 | — | All 446 cortical regions except the 50 tuning regions (@sec-data-synthetic) | — |
| Repetitions per region | — | 4 | — | Independent noise draws per source region, set by power analysis (@sec-annex-power) | — |

: Simulation parameters of Study I. A dash in the Ref. column marks a value we set ourselves; for the amplitude decay $\rho$, which we did not tune, no literature value exists. {#tbl-annex-sim-params}


#### Spike Waveform {#sec-annex-spike}

The spike waveform is a double Hanning window, constructed as in @dewouters_source-reconstructed_2026: a positive Hanning window over the first two thirds of the spike, followed by a negative one of half the amplitude over the last third,

$$
s_0(t) = \begin{cases} h\!\left(t,\, \tfrac{2}{3}W\right) & 0 \leq t \leq \tfrac{2}{3}W, \\[4pt] -\tfrac{1}{2}\,h\!\left(t - \tfrac{2}{3}W,\; \tfrac{1}{3}W\right) & \tfrac{2}{3}W < t \leq W, \end{cases}
$$

where $h(t, T) = \frac{1}{2}\!\left[1 - \cos\!\left(\tfrac{2\pi t}{T}\right)\right]$ is a Hanning window of duration $T$. We set the total duration to $W = 50$ ms, within the 20–70 ms range that defines an interictal spike in clinical EEG [@kane_revised_2017].

#### Propagation Model {#sec-annex-propagation}

A neural mass model [@jansen_electroencephalogram_1995] would describe propagation more physiologically, but networks of neural masses become unstable when they contain many masses, because network size and coupling strength jointly determine their dynamical stability [@sanz-leon_mathematical_2015]. Source-reconstruction studies that use such models therefore typically cap the number of masses at about 1,000, with dipoles roughly 1 cm apart [@siu_structural_2026]. At that spacing, the forward model's point-dipole assumption starts to break down [@nunez_multi-scale_2019]. Our patch-seeded, connectome-driven propagation model avoids this trade-off: it keeps the source space at high resolution (~7,600 dipoles, ~3.3 mm spacing) and remains simple enough to generate realistic EEG spikes. We do not claim that it is more faithful to reality than neural mass or field models, only that it provides insight that a simple patch simulation cannot, while remaining tractable at high dipole counts.

Let $\mathcal S$ be the dipoles of the initial patch. Each dipole $j$ sums attenuated, delayed copies of the spike waveform $s_0$ (@sec-annex-spike), one from each patch dipole $k$:

$$
s_j(t) = \sum_{k \in \mathcal S} \rho^{h_{kj}}\, s_0(t - \tau_{kj}),
$$

where $h_{kj}$ is the number of hops from $k$ to $j$, $\rho = 0.5$ is the amplitude decay per hop, and $\tau_{kj}$ is the propagation delay, with $h_{kk} = \tau_{kk} = 0$. The SNR calibration then sets the overall amplitude (@tbl-annex-sim-params). The delay is the sum of per-edge delays along a path $\mathcal P_{kj}$, plus a jitter term $\epsilon_{kj}$:

$$
\tau_{kj} = \sum_{(u,v)\,\in\,\mathcal{P}_{kj}} \!\left(\frac{l_{uv}}{v(l_{uv})} + \tau_p\right) + \epsilon_{kj},
\qquad
v(l) = \begin{cases} v_{\text{long}} = 4.5 \text{ mm/ms} & l > l_U, \\ v_U = 2.5 \text{ mm/ms} & l \leq l_U, \end{cases}
$$

where $l_{uv}$ is the fiber length of edge $(u,v)$ and $l_U = 30$ mm is the U-fiber length cutoff. Each edge thus contributes a conduction delay, which depends on its length, and a fixed nodal delay $\tau_p$.

The path $\mathcal P_{kj}$ is the one with the smallest total delay. We found it with Dijkstra's algorithm on the connectome, weighting each edge by $l_{uv}/v(l_{uv}) + \tau_p$, without jitter, and computed it separately for every patch dipole $k$. Every dipole is reachable from every patch. The delay, the attenuation and the jitter are all taken along this one path, so $h_{kj}$ counts the relays the activity actually passes through. Because the fastest route can avoid slow edges by taking extra relays, $h_{kj}$ can exceed the smallest number of edges between $k$ and $j$.

For long-range tracts, $v_{\text{long}} = 4.5$ mm/ms (4.5 m/s) is the central value of the ~3–6 m/s that two large cortico-cortical evoked potential (CCEP) studies independently report for adult long-range association fibers [@lemarechal_brain_2022; @van_blooijs_developmental_2023]. U-fibers conduct more slowly, at ~2–3 m/s [@van_blooijs_developmental_2023], so we set $v_U = 2.5$ mm/ms. The nodal delay $\tau_p = 7$ ms represents synaptic transmission plus relay latency at each hop. It is consistent with the population-level excitatory and inhibitory synaptic time constants (5.8–7.3 ms) estimated from CCEP modeling [@lemarechal_brain_2022].

The jitter term models uncertainty in propagation timing. We draw it independently for each pair $(k, j)$, as $\epsilon_{kj} \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\, h_{kj} \sigma_\tau^2)$ with $\sigma_\tau = 1$ ms. Its variance thus grows with the number of hops, as if independent per-hop jitters were summed, but dipoles reached through the same edge do not share a draw.

We separated consecutive spikes by 1 s, so that propagation ends before the next spike begins. Without jitter, the longest delay from a patch dipole to any dipole is 127 ms across Study I's 396 regions (median over regions 112 ms), and in every region, 99% of the propagated amplitude arrives within 108 ms. With the 50 ms waveform, activity therefore ends within about 180 ms of onset, well before the next spike. Consistent with this, the baseline of the averaged EEG showed no propagated activity.


#### Noise Model {#sec-annex-noise}

The sensor-level noise has two components. First, every dipole receives its own pink noise (power ∝ 1/f), drawn independently across dipoles and runs. This noise is spatially uncorrelated at the sources. Second, every channel receives white noise of 2.0 µV RMS, representing the instrument and electrode noise floor. We scaled the source noise so that the total baseline noise reaches 15.0 µV RMS, the midpoint of the ~10–20 µV RMS range commonly reported for scalp EEG background activity [@nunez_electric_2006]. Because the two components add in quadrature, the source part contributes about 14.9 µV RMS.

We calibrated both the noise and the SNR on a single channel: the one on which the noise-free spike is largest. On this channel, the SNR of a spike is its peak absolute amplitude within ±30 ms of onset, divided by the standard deviation of the baseline (−450 to −200 ms). The SNR of a run is the median over its 20 spikes. We scaled the source activity, before projecting it to the sensors, iteratively on the same noise draw until the run's SNR was within 5% of the target of 5.

This per-spike SNR lies somewhat above the ~2.0–3.2 (as amplitude ratios) reported for single interictal spikes [@gonsisko_electroencephalographic_2024]. The noise analysis (@sec-s1-data-noise; full results in @sec-annex-s1-data-noise) covers SNRs from 1 to 20. All metrics, however, use each run's average of its 20 spikes, which has a higher SNR: on the calibration channel, the median over the 1,584 runs is 21.5 (IQR 19.0–24.0, range 12.1–40.0), consistent with the $5\sqrt{20} \approx 22$ expected for independent noise.

### Epilepsy Surgery Data (Study II) {#sec-annex-resection}

This section provides additional detail for the epilepsy surgery cohort described in @sec-data-resection.

#### Preprocessing by the Data Providers {#sec-annex-resection-preprocessing}

The data providers preprocessed the EEG before release, as described by @vorderwulbecke_high-density_2025. Because the dataset was collected longitudinally, the filter settings vary across patients: the high-pass cutoff ranges from 0.3 to 1 Hz and the low-pass cutoff from 30 to 100 Hz. The providers also downsampled the data to 250 Hz and interpolated noisy channels from neighboring electrodes with 3D splines.

The dataset is provided in two channel versions: the full 257-channel HydroCel Geodesic Sensor Net and a 204-channel version without the cheek and neck electrodes. We used the 204-channel version, the same montage as in the simulations (@sec-annex-processing).

#### Resection Masks {#sec-annex-resection-masks}

**RAMPS.** We first segmented every resection with RAMPS [@simpson_automated_2025], which compares the pre-operative and the skull-stripped post-operative T1-weighted MRI and returns the resected volume as a mask in pre-operative space. RAMPS requires the hemisphere and lobe of the resection as input. We took the hemisphere from the dataset's clinical metadata. The metadata also state whether each resection was temporal or extratemporal. For the 9 extratemporal resections, we identified the lobe (frontal, parietal or parieto-occipital) visually on the post-operative MRI.

**Quality control.** The first author, who is not a clinician, overlaid each mask on both MRIs and accepted it if it matched the resection cavity, the dark region that the resection leaves on the post-operative MRI. RAMPS gave an acceptable mask for 21 of the 26 patients. For the other 5, its mask did not match the cavity (3 patients), it produced no output (1 patient), it could not run because the post-operative image was a CT rather than a T1-weighted MRI (1 patient). The patient for whom RAMPS produced no output has no visible cavity on the post-operative MRI, so we excluded this patient from the study.

**Replacement masks.** For these 5 patients, we used masks that we segmented semi-manually. For the 4 patients, including the one with a post-operative CT, we outlined the resection by hand on every third slice of the pre-operative T1-weighted MRI. We filled each slice in between from the nearest outlined slice, propagating its outline with nonlinear (SyN) registration [@avants_symmetric_2008]. The first author checked these replacement masks visually in the same way as the RAMPS masks.


### Simultaneous EEG–iEEG Data (Study III) {#sec-annex-data-ieeg}

This section provides additional recruitment, implantation, and ethics detail for the simultaneous EEG/iEEG cohort described in @sec-data-ieeg, drawn from @roehri_scalp-negative_2025, the source study for this cohort.

#### Recruitment and Implantation {#sec-annex-ieeg-recruitment}

Patients were recruited at the EEG and Epilepsy Unit of Geneva University Hospital, among consecutive patients who underwent simultaneous iEEG–EEG recording between 2014 and 2019 during presurgical evaluation for pharmacoresistant focal epilepsy. The intracranial recordings used stereo-EEG (SEEG) macroelectrodes, implanted according to clinical presurgical planning. The simultaneous recording took place on the last day before the intracranial electrodes were removed and combined the SEEG with a 257-channel geodesic scalp EEG net (Electrical Geodesics, Inc.).

The EEG was provided to us with 208 channels: the 204 channels used in Studies I and II, plus electrodes E67, E219, E225 and E253. @roehri_scalp-negative_2025 do not describe how the 257 channels were reduced to 208. We computed the forward model for all 208 channels and used all of them for reconstruction.

#### Ethics Approval {#sec-annex-ieeg-ethics}

The study was approved by the Geneva Regional Research Ethics Committee (protocol 13-004). @roehri_scalp-negative_2025 report that the patients agreed to take part in the simultaneous recording procedure, but do not state whether consent was given in writing.

#### Comparison Window {#sec-annex-ieeg-window}

We compared virtual and recorded iEEG over a window defined on the recorded iEEG. We first computed its global field power (GFP), the standard deviation across contacts of the iEEG averaged over spikes. The threshold was the mean of the GFP over a baseline 0.5–1.0 s into each 4 s epoch, plus 3 standard deviations. We took the intervals during which the GFP exceeded this threshold, filled gaps shorter than 100 ms, dropped intervals shorter than 20 ms, and kept the longest remaining interval. In all four patients, this interval contained the GFP maximum and lasted 510–1,510 ms. Patients 12 and 48 also had shorter suprathreshold intervals, near the epoch edges and after the spike, which this rule excludes.

## Evaluation Metrics {#sec-annex-metrics}

### Localization Error {#sec-annex-loc}

Localization error depends on when it is measured. Early in the spike, the active region is still small, but the EEG is weak relative to the noise. At the peak of the EEG, the SNR is highest, but the activity has usually spread beyond its origin. Measuring at a fixed fraction of the peak amplitude balances the two. Defining this fraction on the EEG rather than on the sources lets us find the time point in the same way for simulated and clinical data, where the sources are unknown.

We determine this time point once per spike, on the averaged EEG, and use it for every method. We first locate the peak: the channel and sample with the largest absolute amplitude within a search window. On that channel, the time point is the first sample between the start of the search window and the peak at which the absolute amplitude reaches a set fraction of the peak amplitude.

In Study I, the fraction is 25% and the search window is the reconstruction window (−20 to 150 ms), so that a noise fluctuation elsewhere in the epoch cannot be mistaken for the peak. The main analysis and the connectome-degradation analysis take the time point from the noisy averaged EEG, the same signal that is reconstructed. The noise-robustness analysis instead takes it from each run's noise-free EEG, so that the time point does not move with the noise level and all methods are compared at the same instant at every SNR. In Study II, the fraction is 50%, the value that @vorderwulbecke_high-density_2020 found most accurate on this dataset, and the search window is the whole averaged spike.

### Additional iEEG Metrics {#sec-annex-iEEG-metrics}

For comparison with earlier simultaneous EEG–iEEG studies, we report two further measures of agreement between the virtual and the recorded iEEG (results in @sec-annex-s3-correlation). Both use the same data as the main metric: the averaged recorded and virtual iEEG, each normalized by its standard deviation over the baseline (0.5–1.0 s), at every sample of the comparison window (@sec-annex-ieeg-window).

**Spatial correlation at the peak.** @grova_intracranial_2016 compared the two signals over five samples around the spike peak. We therefore also average the spatial correlation (@sec-metric-corr) over the five samples (±10 ms at 200 Hz) centered on the peak of the recorded iEEG. The peak is the sample within the comparison window at which the GFP of the normalized recorded iEEG is largest. This GFP differs from the one that defines the comparison window, which is computed on the raw averaged iEEG (@sec-annex-ieeg-window). The two maxima fall on the same sample in three of the four patients and 25 ms apart in the fourth (patient 50).

**AUC.** The area under the ROC curve (AUC) measures how well the virtual iEEG separates active from inactive contacts [@grova_evaluation_2006]; we compute it as in @afnan_assessing_2026. At each sample, a contact is active if its absolute recorded amplitude reaches at least 30% of the largest absolute amplitude across contacts at that sample. The AUC is then the probability that an active contact has a larger absolute virtual amplitude than an inactive one, with ties counted as one half. It is 0.5 at chance and 1 for perfect separation. Because it uses only absolute amplitudes, the AUC ignores the sign of each contact. This matters because the sign can flip for geometric reasons, for example when the generator lies outside the cortical source space or when a contact lies very close to it. As for the spatial correlation, we report the AUC averaged over the comparison window and over the five samples around the peak.

**Chance level.** For each patient and method, we permute the contacts of the virtual iEEG randomly 1,000 times, applying the same permutation at every sample, as in @afnan_assessing_2026. We recompute both measures for each permutation. The 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the 1,000 values give the range expected by chance.

## Statistical Analysis {#sec-annex-stats}

### Power Analysis {#sec-annex-power}

We chose the number of regions and of runs per region for Study I from a pilot. The pilot used the 50 tuning regions (@sec-annex-tuning), none of which appears in Study I, with 4 runs each, which we simulated and analyzed exactly as in Study I. The design had to reach a power of 0.90 on every comparison, with the pilot setting the direction of each test. For localization error, wCSET was slightly worse than CSET and dSPM in the pilot, so we required non-inferiority against these two methods and superiority against sLORETA and wMNE. For spatial correlation, we required superiority against all four methods, assuming half the pilot's average difference. We estimated power for 50 to 396 regions and 1 to 8 runs per region with a two-stage bootstrap of the pilot that resampled regions and then runs within regions.

Only the non-inferiority tests constrained the design: with 396 regions, every other test had a power close to 1 even with a single run per region. For non-inferiority, adding regions raises power more than adding runs does, because the variance between regions dominates. For the same total of about 1,600 runs, 200 regions × 8 runs gave a power of only 0.68 against CSET, whereas 396 regions × 4 runs gave 0.91. We therefore used every cortical region not used for tuning (396 of 446) and the fewest runs that met the target: 4 runs, which gave a power of 0.91 against CSET and 0.96 against dSPM.

### Cluster-Based Permutation Tests {#sec-annex-cluster}

For outcomes that vary along a continuous dimension (time, SNR or perturbation severity), we compared wCSET with each method using a cluster-based permutation test [@maris_nonparametric_2007], as implemented in MNE-Python (`permutation_cluster_1samp_test`). The test's unit is the region: for each region, we averaged the difference between wCSET and the method over the region's runs, which gave one difference series per region.

At each point of the dimension, we tested these differences across regions with a one-sample t-test. Adjacent points whose t-values exceeded the two-tailed threshold for p < 0.05 formed a cluster, with positive and negative differences clustered separately. A cluster's mass is the sum of its t-values. To build the null distribution, we randomly flipped the sign of each region's entire difference series, repeated this 3,000 times, and recorded the largest cluster mass in each permutation. A cluster's p-value is the proportion of permutations whose largest mass equalled or exceeded that cluster's mass. Because 3,000 permutations estimate very small p-values imprecisely, we report values below 0.001 as p < 0.001.

For each method, we kept its most significant cluster and corrected these p-values across the methods of a family with the Holm procedure. The test controls the false-positive rate for the claim that a difference exists somewhere along the dimension, not for the claim that it exists at any given point. We therefore report a cluster's start and end as approximate. To estimate the size of each significant difference, we averaged each region's difference over the cluster's extent and summarized these averages across regions (@sec-stats-tests). For localization error, we report the Hodges–Lehmann estimate with its distribution-free CI. For spatial correlation, we report the mean with its t-based CI.

### Spike Bootstrap (Study III) {#sec-annex-bootstrap}

**Why a bootstrap.** In Study III, each patient provides a single averaged spike, so there is no sample of independent observations on which to compare methods. The time points of the averaged spike cannot serve as observations either, because they are too autocorrelated. The independent units are the individual spikes. We therefore estimated the uncertainty of each comparison by resampling spikes, separately for each patient [@field_bootstrapping_2007].

**Resampling units.** Spikes close in time are not independent. When the comparison window of one spike overlaps the baseline of a later spike, the earlier spike's signal enters the later spike's normalization. The spikes were exported as 4 s epochs without timestamps, so we detected this overlap from the samples that two epochs share. We grouped into a burst all spikes linked by overlap, directly or through a chain of other spikes, and resampled whole bursts, a cluster bootstrap [@cameron_bootstrap-based_2008]. Patients 1–4 had 265, 200, 257 and 130 spikes, in 210, 170, 195 and 117 bursts.

**One draw.** In each of 1,000 draws, we sampled bursts with replacement, as many as the patient had, using a fixed random seed per patient. We then averaged the selected spikes in both EEG and iEEG, reconstructed the average with every method, and computed the spatial correlation between virtual and recorded iEEG as in the main analysis (@sec-metric-corr). We kept the noise covariance, regularization parameter, comparison window and peak samples at their values from all spikes. All methods used the same draws, and we computed the difference between wCSET and each method within each draw, so the bootstrap is paired. Applied to all spikes, this pipeline reproduced the main analysis.

**Estimate and interval.** The estimate of each difference, $\hat\theta$, is the difference observed on the average of all spikes. The draws, however, are biased toward zero. A resampled average contains fewer distinct spikes, so it is noisier, and noise lowers the correlation of every method with the recorded iEEG, which shrinks the differences between methods. In our data, this bias reached 1.1 bootstrap standard errors. A percentile interval would inherit it, so we used the basic interval [@davison_bootstrap_1997], $[2\hat\theta - \theta^*_{1-\alpha/2},\ 2\hat\theta - \theta^*_{\alpha/2}]$, where $\theta^*_q$ is the $q$-quantile of the draws. The basic interval reflects the draws around $\hat\theta$, so a shift of the draws toward zero moves the interval away from zero by the same amount.

**p-value.** We obtained the p-value by inverting the same interval. We counted the reflected draws ($2\hat\theta - \theta^*$) on each side of zero, added one to each count, divided by 1,001, and doubled the smaller share. For each patient, we Holm-corrected the five comparisons with wCSET (@sec-stats-tests). The smallest attainable p-value, 2/1,001 ≈ 0.002, lies below the strictest Holm threshold for five comparisons (0.01), so 1,000 draws are enough to reach significance. We report 99% CIs, which match that strictest threshold. These CIs are conservative: a comparison can be significant after Holm correction while its 99% CI still includes zero.

def _snr_order(metric):
    return sorted(noise_metrics.to_df(metrics=metric, filters={"phase": "qrp"})["snr"].unique(), reverse=True)

def _noise_test(metric, phase, higher_is_better):
    return cached(
        noise_metrics.stat.cluster_permutation, f"../results/simf/noise_sweep/stats/{metric}_{phase}_cluster",
        metric, coord="snr", group_by="Method",

_loc_medians = _noise_medians("localization_error", "qrp")

    """Largest cluster of the given sign (+1 = wCSET better) against `competitor`, or None."""
    clusters = result.clusters_by_pair[("wcset", competitor)]
    rows = clusters[clusters["sign"] == sign] if not clusters.empty else clusters
    return None if rows.empty else main_cluster(rows)

CI_LEVEL = 0.99  # as in the main text: CIs Bonferroni-corrected for families of up to five comparisons

    """Paired difference over a cluster's SNR span, positive = wCSET better, with its 99% CI: the Hodges-Lehmann
    estimate for localization error and the mean for correlation, as in the main text."""
    snrs = [v for v in _snr_order(metric) if cluster["snr_end"] <= v <= cluster["snr_start"]]
    estimator = noise_metrics.estimate.hodges_lehmann if metric == "localization_error" else noise_metrics.estimate.mean_diff
    return estimator(
        metric, group_by="Method", comparisons=[("wcset", competitor)], pairing_col="region",
        filters={"phase": phase, "snr": snrs}, alpha=1 - CI_LEVEL,
    ).vs("wcset", higher_is_better=higher_is_better).loc[competitor]

def _p(p_corrected):

_df_loc = noise_metrics.to_df(metrics="localization_error", filters={"phase": "qrp"})
noise_n_regions = _df_loc["region"].nunique()

noise_snr_levels = ", ".join(f"{v:g}" for v in _snr_order("localization_error"))

# Localization error: the significant clusters of each pair and direction (sign +1 = wCSET better), from high to
# low SNR, and the paired difference over each cluster's span with its p, e.g. "3.9 mm (99% CI 2.8 to 5.0;

def _clusters(competitor, sign, significant=True):
    clusters = noise_loc_results.clusters_by_pair[("wcset", competitor)]
    if clusters.empty:

    return f'{fmt_ci(est, "estimate", unit=" mm", level=CI_LEVEL)[:-1]}; p_corrected {_p(cluster["p_corrected"])})'

We repeated the Study I simulation for all `{python} noise_n_regions` regions at single-spike SNRs of `{python} noise_snr_levels`, with `{python} noise_n_runs` runs per region at each SNR (@sec-data-synthetic). The tests are those of the main text: each region is summarized by the mean over its runs, and a cluster-based permutation test over SNR compares wCSET with each competitor, region-paired and Holm-corrected across the four competitors. Over each cluster's SNR span, differences in localization error are Hodges–Lehmann shifts and differences in spatial correlation are mean paired differences, both positive when wCSET is better. The figures show the median across regions.

At SNR 20, wCSET, CSET, sLORETA and dSPM all localized well, with median errors of `{python} noise_loc_four_20_lo`–`{python} noise_loc_four_20_hi` mm (@fig-annex-noise-loc). wMNE started at `{python} noise_loc_wmne_median20` mm but degraded first: its median rose to `{python} noise_loc_wmne_median5` mm at SNR 5 and `{python} noise_loc_wmne_median1` mm at SNR 1, and wCSET localized more accurately than wMNE at every SNR, by `{python} noise_loc_wmne`. The other four methods degraded later and reached `{python} noise_loc_four_1_lo`–`{python} noise_loc_four_1_hi` mm at SNR 1. At high SNR, wCSET had the lowest median error (`{python} noise_loc_wcset_high_lo`–`{python} noise_loc_wcset_high_hi` mm from SNR 20 to 10) and localized more accurately than dSPM from SNR 20 to `{python} noise_loc_dspm_better_end`, by `{python} noise_loc_dspm_better`, and than CSET from SNR 20 to `{python} noise_loc_cset_better_end`, by `{python} noise_loc_cset_better`. Against sLORETA, whose median errors were close to wCSET's at high SNR, the difference was not significant at SNR `{python} noise_loc_sloreta_ns_snr` (p_corrected `{python} noise_loc_sloreta_ns_p`) and formed no cluster at SNR 14 and 10. wCSET's median error rose from `{python} noise_loc_wcset_median10` mm at SNR 10 to `{python} noise_loc_wcset_median5` mm at SNR 5, whereas dSPM's stayed at `{python} noise_loc_dspm_median_lo`–`{python} noise_loc_dspm_median_hi` mm from SNR 20 down to 5. dSPM was therefore more accurate than wCSET from SNR `{python} noise_loc_dspm_worse_start` to `{python} noise_loc_dspm_worse_end`, by `{python} noise_loc_dspm_worse`, with the largest gap at SNR `{python} noise_loc_gap_snr` (medians `{python} noise_loc_gap_dspm` vs. `{python} noise_loc_gap_wcset` mm). CSET was more accurate than wCSET from SNR `{python} noise_loc_cset_worse_start` to `{python} noise_loc_cset_worse_end`, by `{python} noise_loc_cset_worse`, and from SNR `{python} noise_loc_cset_worse2_start` to `{python} noise_loc_cset_worse2_end`, by `{python} noise_loc_cset_worse2`; at SNR `{python} noise_loc_cset_ns_snr`, wCSET was the more accurate of the two, but not significantly (p_corrected `{python} noise_loc_cset_ns_p`). sLORETA degraded faster than wCSET below SNR 10, and wCSET was more accurate than sLORETA from SNR `{python} noise_loc_sloreta_start` to `{python} noise_loc_sloreta_end`, by `{python} noise_loc_sloreta`.

Spatial correlation separated the methods more clearly (@fig-annex-noise-corr). wCSET's median correlation fell from `{python} noise_corr_wcset_qrp20` at the quarter rising phase and `{python} noise_corr_wcset_pp20` at the peak at SNR 20 to `{python} noise_corr_wcset_qrp1` at SNR 1. CSET followed the same course at lower values (`{python} noise_corr_cset_pp20` at the peak at SNR 20), whereas the minimum-norm methods stayed between `{python} noise_corr_std_lo` and `{python} noise_corr_std_hi` across the whole range. From SNR 20, wCSET's correlation was higher than the minimum-norm methods' down to SNR `{python} noise_corr_end_std` and than CSET's down to SNR `{python} noise_corr_end_cset`, at both phases (all p_corrected `{python} noise_corr_p_max`). Over these clusters, it exceeded the minimum-norm methods' by Δr = `{python} noise_corr_std_d_lo`–`{python} noise_corr_std_d_hi` and CSET's by Δr = `{python} noise_corr_cset_d_qrp` at the quarter rising phase and `{python} noise_corr_cset_d_pp` at the peak. At the lowest SNRs, the spike could no longer be distinguished from the noise. wCSET's and CSET's correlations fell to at most `{python} noise_corr_cw_1_hi`, whereas the minimum-norm methods' leveled off at `{python} noise_corr_std_1_lo`–`{python} noise_corr_std_1_hi`, so wCSET's was slightly lower than theirs (Δr = `{python} noise_corr_worse_std_lo`–`{python} noise_corr_worse_std_hi`) and differed from CSET's by less than 0.01 (all p_corrected ≤ `{python} noise_corr_worse_p_max`).

### CSET and wCSET keep their correlation advantage despite large connectome errors {#sec-annex-s1-prior-noise}

Full results of the connectome perturbation experiment summarized in @sec-s1-prior-noise.

```{python filename="simf_degradation_stats.py"}
#| output: false
import mindmap as mm
import numpy as np

deg_metrics = mm.metric.MetricSuite.load("../results/simf/degradation")

# Same tests as the main text (index.qmd, simf_degradation_summary_stats.py), reloaded from its cache: cluster
# permutation over perturbation level, CSET/wCSET vs. each connectome-agnostic reference (sLORETA, dSPM),
# region-paired (each region = the mean over its runs), Holm across the 4 pairs (family="pair"). Localization
# error at the quarter rising phase, spatial correlation at the peak. The reference comes first in each pair, so
# sign = -1 means CSET/wCSET is better.
DEG_PHASE = {"localization_error": "qrp", "correlation": "pp"}
DEG_REFERENCES = ["sloreta", "dspm"]

def _deg_test(metric, higher_is_better):
    phase = DEG_PHASE[metric]
    order = sorted(deg_metrics.to_df(metrics=metric, filters={"phase": phase})["percentage"].unique())
    return cached(
        deg_metrics.stat.cluster_permutation, f"../results/simf/degradation/stats/{metric}_{phase}_cluster",
        metric, coord="percentage", group_by="Method",
        comparisons=deg_metrics.stat.build_comparisons(DEG_REFERENCES, ["cset", "wcset"]),
        pairing_col="region", coord_order=order, higher_is_better=higher_is_better, filters={"phase": phase},
        correction="holm", family="pair", n_permutations=3000, seed=0,
    )

deg_results = {"localization_error": _deg_test("localization_error", False), "correlation": _deg_test("correlation", True)}
deg_n_regions = deg_metrics.to_df(metrics="localization_error")["region"].nunique()
```

```{python filename="simf_degradation_plot.py"}
#| echo: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

DEG_METHODS = ["wcset", "cset", "sloreta", "dspm"]
DEG_PAIRS = [("sloreta", "wcset"), ("dspm", "wcset"), ("sloreta", "cset"), ("dspm", "cset")]

def degradation_figure(metric, ylabel):
    """Median across regions (each region = the mean over its runs) with an IQR band per method, and below it one
    row of significant clusters per pair (colored: CSET/wCSET better than the reference, gray: worse)."""
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 5))
    deg_metrics.plot.line(
        metric, "percentage", hue="Method", unit="region", hue_order=DEG_METHODS, center="median", interval="iqr",
        highlight="wcset", palette=COLORS, fill_alpha=0.15, labels=METHOD_LABELS, filters={"phase": DEG_PHASE[metric]},
        ax=ax,
    )
    ax.legend(*ax.get_legend_handles_labels(), loc="center left", bbox_to_anchor=(1.0, 0.6), fontsize=8, frameon=False)
    result = deg_results[metric]
    levels = np.asarray(result.coord_order, dtype=float)
    step = (levels[1] - levels[0]) / 2
    dy = np.ptp(ax.get_ylim())
    row_h, row0 = 0.035 * dy, ax.get_ylim()[0] - 0.04 * dy
    for k, (ref, method) in enumerate(DEG_PAIRS):
        y = row0 - (k + 1) * 1.4 * row_h
        cl = result.clusters_by_pair[(ref, method)]
        for _, row in cl[cl["significant"].astype(bool)].iterrows():
            better = row["sign"] < 0
            ax.fill_between([row["percentage_start"] - step, row["percentage_end"] + step], y, y + row_h,
                            color=matte(COLORS[method]) if better else "#c3c2b7", linewidth=0, zorder=2)
        ax.text(levels[0] - 2 * step, y + row_h / 2, f"{METHOD_LABELS[method]} vs. {METHOD_LABELS[ref]}", fontsize=7,
                ha="right", va="center", color="#444444")
    yticks = [v for v in ax.get_yticks() if row0 <= v <= ax.get_ylim()[1]]
    ax.set_ylim(row0 - (len(DEG_PAIRS) + 0.6) * 1.4 * row_h, ax.get_ylim()[1])
    ax.set_yticks(yticks)
    ax.set_xticks(levels)
    ax.set_xlabel("Connectome edges swapped (%)")
    ax.set_ylabel(ylabel)
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
    fig.tight_layout()
    return fig
```
